notes: The early-pathways curriculum for the Trades Network: the working world brought into the subjects a school already teaches, from K–2 up. Five tracks — discovering the trades early, the math on the jobsite, the science in the craft, reading and writing the working word, and civics through the working city — so a district can teach fractions on a cut list, energy on a live-wire hazard map (never a live wire), and civic history through its own port and union halls. Transfer checks stay on real material a classroom can hold: rulers, recipes, water, paper specs, public records and observation from safe, public ground. The honesty stances carry verbatim: no union local numbers (the regional council is the front door) and no classroom activity ever counts as equipment certification or union credit.

themes.description: Streets, mains, wires, levees — a city as the sum of finished jobs, most of them invisible until they fail.
themes.transfer_check: Walk one block and list ten pieces of built work in order of what would be missed first if it stopped.

bands.K–2: Walk around and point out three things that were built by someone.
bands.3–5: Walk one block and list five pieces of built work you see.
bands.6–8: Walk one block and list ten pieces of built work in order of importance, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Walk one block and list ten pieces of built work in order of what would be missed first if it failed.
bands.11–12: Survey a real block's infrastructure and rank it by consequence of failure, verified against a real utility map.

themes.description: Bonds, budgets, councils and boards — the civic machinery that turns taxes into pump stations and schools.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real public project in your parish or city budget and name the body that approved it and the money that funds it.

bands.K–2: Say who decides if a new park or school gets built in your town.
bands.3–5: Find out who decides what gets built in your town — a council, a vote, a budget.
bands.6–8: Find one real public project and name the body that decided it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find one real public project in your parish or city budget and name the body that decided to fund it.
bands.11–12: Trace a real public project from its decision-making body through its budget line, verified against public records.

themes.theme: A short history of the union
themes.description: Why workers organized — hours, safety, the wage — and what apprenticeship halls did for the people who built your city.
themes.transfer_check: Tell the story of one real historical labor milestone, from a source you can name, to somebody who hadn't heard it.

bands.K–2: Say why workers might join together to ask for safer conditions.
bands.3–5: Find one story about workers organizing for something fair, like safety or pay.
bands.6–8: Tell the story of one real historical labor milestone, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Tell the story of one real historical labor milestone, from a source you can name.
bands.11–12: Research and present one real labor milestone with a named, verifiable source and its lasting effect.

themes.description: New Orleans on its river, Oakland on its bay, San Francisco on its gate — how working water shaped where people live.
themes.transfer_check: For one of the network's regions, explain from a map why the city stands where it does and what still moves through it.

bands.K–2: Say why a city near water might have grown up right there.
bands.3–5: Find why one city on the network map is located where it is, near water.
bands.6–8: Explain from a map why one network city stands where it does, with a checker.
bands.9–10: For one of the network's regions, explain from a map why the city stands where it does.
bands.11–12: Explain, with real geographic evidence, why a real port city's location shaped its economy and layout.

themes.theme: The strike, the deal and the contract
themes.description: How disagreement at work becomes negotiation — the contract as a civic document both sides sign and both sides keep.
themes.transfer_check: Role-play a two-side negotiation over a classroom rule to a written one-line agreement both sides initial.

bands.K–2: Say what two people should do when they disagree about something: talk it out.
bands.3–5: Role-play two sides disagreeing about a rule and reaching an agreement.
bands.6–8: Role-play a two-side negotiation over a classroom rule to a written agreement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Role-play a two-side negotiation over a classroom rule to a written one-line agreement.
bands.11–12: Role-play a real-style labor negotiation to a written, signed agreement both sides accept.

themes.description: Codes, permits and inspections as public promises — why the stamp on the drawing protects people who never read it.
themes.transfer_check: Explain, using one real example (an elevator plate, a restaurant grade, a permit), who inspected it and who is protected.

bands.K–2: Say why someone checks that a building or ride is safe before people use it.
bands.3–5: Find a real inspection sticker or stamp and say what it promises.
bands.6–8: Explain, using one real example, what an inspection stamp protects, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, using one real example (an elevator plate, a restaurant grade, a permit), what the stamp protects and for whom.
bands.11–12: Explain a real inspection or code system, verified against the actual regulation it enforces.

themes.description: Who restores the grid, drains the street, reopens the school — the working city's emergency shape, from Gulf hurricanes to Bay quakes.
themes.transfer_check: Chart which crews, in what order, brought one real past storm's neighborhood back — from news or a firsthand account.

bands.K–2: Say who comes to help fix things after a big storm.
bands.3–5: List three kinds of workers who help a town recover after a storm.
bands.6–8: Chart which crews restored one real past storm's neighborhood, in order, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Chart which crews, in what order, brought one real past storm's neighborhood back online.
bands.11–12: Chart a real storm recovery timeline by crew and order, verified against a real news or utility account.

themes.description: Who historically got the good trades and who was kept out — and what halls, schools and laws have done to open the door.
themes.transfer_check: Compare an old and a new photograph or roster of the same trade and describe, with respect, what changed and what still should.

bands.K–2: Say why it is fair for anyone, no matter who they are, to be able to try a job.
bands.3–5: Compare an old photo of workers to a new one and say what changed.
bands.6–8: Compare an old and a new photograph or roster of the same trade, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare an old and a new photograph or roster of the same trade and describe what changed and why.
bands.11–12: Compare real historical and current workforce data for a trade and describe honestly what opened the door.

themes.description: Apprenticeship as a public institution — registered programs, journey cards, and the taxes and codes that stand behind them.
themes.transfer_check: Chart the registered apprenticeship path for one trade in your region from the program's own public materials.

bands.K–2: Say what steps someone climbs to become really good at a job over time.
bands.3–5: Chart the steps of becoming a trained worker in one trade, from beginner to expert.
bands.6–8: Chart the registered apprenticeship path for one trade in your region, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Chart the registered apprenticeship path for one trade in your region from the public registry.
bands.11–12: Chart and verify a real registered apprenticeship path against its public registry and the codes that stand behind it.

themes.theme: Your seat in the working city
themes.description: The learner as a future voter, neighbor and maybe tradesperson — where to stand on the next bond, the next hall, the next storm.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real public meeting that touches built work and report the one decision you would have voted on, and how.

bands.K–2: Say one thing you could vote on or care about when you grow up in your town.
bands.3–5: Say one real local decision you might one day have a say in as a voter.
bands.6–8: Attend or watch one real public meeting that touches built work, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Attend or watch one real public meeting that touches built work and report what was decided.
bands.11–12: Attend a real public meeting on built work and report the decision and where you would stand on the next one.
